subject: Business Models
title: Two-Sided Markets
description: A micro-lesson that makes Two-Sided Markets usable.

hook.text: A credit card is useless without merchants. Merchants won't accept cards nobody carries. Who goes first?

buildup.text: Two-sided markets serve two distinct user groups who need each other to create value.

discovery.text: The platform's job is to subsidize one side to attract the other. Visa subsidized cardholders first.

twist.text: Once critical mass is reached on both sides, the platform becomes nearly impossible to displace.

climax.text: Google, Uber, and Airbnb all serve two-sided markets. Each side makes the other more valuable.

punchline.text: Two sides, one platform in the middle collecting fees.

quiz.question: How do platforms typically solve the two-sided market problem?
options: Subsidize one side to attract the other

details.summary: Two-sided markets are platforms that serve two distinct user groups who provide each other with network benefits. Credit cards connect merchants and cardholders, newspapers connect readers and advertisers, and dating apps connect two pools of potential matches.
details.whyItMatters: Two-sided market theory explains why platforms often subsidize one side to attract the other. This pricing asymmetry is fundamental to understanding platform business model design and competitive strategy.
takeaways: Platforms serve two interdependent user groups that need each other
Pricing strategy often subsidizes the more price-sensitive side
The money side pays more because it gains value from the subsidized side

faq.question: Why do platforms often give their product away to one side for free?
faq.answer: The subsidized side's participation creates value that the other side will pay for. Google gives search free to users because their attention is valuable to advertisers. Credit cards reward cardholders because merchant transaction fees fund the system.

faq.question: How do you determine which side of a two-sided market to subsidize?
faq.answer: Generally subsidize the side that is more price-sensitive, harder to attract, or whose participation generates more value for the paying side. The side with more alternatives or lower willingness to pay typically receives subsidies or free access.
